title: Thirteen Quantitative Principles
summary: Explain the physical basis of the Energy-Movement Principle and evaluate how on-chip data reuse and kernel fusion minimize total system energy.

blocks.md:
By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

- Explain the physical basis of the Energy-Movement Principle and evaluate how on-chip data reuse and kernel fusion minimize total system energy
- Distinguish the conservation-of-complexity diagnostic heuristic from exact physical conservation laws
- Identify the conservation-of-complexity heuristic as the overarching diagnostic framework uniting the thirteen quantitative principles
- Analyze how deployment diagnostics (drift, skew, bias feedback) drive the feedback loop from production back to data engineering and retraining in the ML systems lifecycle

blocks.source: Vol I, Conclusion, § Thirteen Quantitative Principles
blocks.md: Whether an engineer alters an embedding table layout in DLRM, doubles batch size in ResNet-50, or quantizes an attention layer from FP16 to INT8, the outcome follows from physical bounds, empirical trade-offs, and operational feedback rather than guesswork. Reasoning about those cross-layer effects before profiling is the job of the **thirteen quantitative principles** the book accumulated across its four parts (a later section).

blocks.title: What the section covers
blocks.md:
In the book this section runs through:

- What shapes predictions (principles 1 and 13)
- What limits execution (principles 2–8)
- What evidence supports deployment (principles 9–12)
- The integrated framework

Pay attention to: the three questions that regroup the principles: what shapes predictions, what limits execution, and what evidence supports deployment; the Energy-Movement Principle and the 100-1,000x DRAM vs. FLOP energy gap; the conservation-of-complexity heuristic as a diagnostic tool to trace displaced burdens; the Deploy-to-Foundations feedback loop in the Cycle of ML Systems.

blocks.prompt: Think first: In the Cycle of ML Systems diagram in @fig-invariants-cycle, the Deploy phase contains an explicit feedback arrow returning to Foundations (Data). Explain what production signals activate this feedback loop and why automated rollback is insufficient when the cause is external statistical drift.
blocks.md: The Deploy-to-Foundations feedback loop is activated by deployment diagnostics: the verification gap (estimating accuracy bounds under real traffic), statistical drift (distribution shifts in input features or user cohorts), training-serving skew (mismatched feature preprocessing paths), and bias feedback amplification. When a drift signal is detected, automated rollback only repairs software regressions caused by faulty code or bad model releases. If the underlying cause is external real-world distribution change (e.g., seasonal shifts, macro trends, or new user populations), rolling back to an older checkpoint trained on even staler data fails to restore accuracy. The feedback arrow requires diagnosing the root cause, collecting newly representative data, revalidating feature pipelines, and retraining or adapting the model.

questions.q: According to the Energy-Movement Principle ($E_{\text{total}} = \sum_j N_j E_j$), accessing off-chip DRAM requires approximately 100 to 1,000 times more energy than executing a single FP16 or FP32 arithmetic operation. What is the direct systems design implication of this physical reality?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is D. Architectures and runtimes should evaluate on-chip reuse and reduced memory traffic, counting accesses at their actual width and arithmetic operations to determine the energy savings. The stated reference ratio compares one DRAM access with one arithmetic operation. An access moves several bytes, so byte volume must be converted to access counts using the actual transfer width. Fusion, tiling, and supported quantization can reduce memory traffic, but the savings depend on the number of accesses removed, changes in arithmetic and runtime costs, and the energy boundary. A whole-system energy estimate or measurement must include the remaining costs; the per-event ratio alone does not establish orders-of-magnitude total savings. The other choices ignore locality or assume energy contributions that the event counts do not establish.
questions.hint: Think about: explain the physical basis of the Energy-Movement Principle and evaluate how on-chip data reuse and kernel fusion minimize total system energy.
options: Inference engines should prioritize minimizing total ALU operations above all else, even if intermediate tensors must be repeatedly written to and read from off-chip DRAM.
Hardware accelerators consume identical energy regardless of whether memory accesses hit on-chip SRAM or off-chip DRAM, because memory controller power is fixed.
Quantization saves energy exclusively by simplifying ALU multiplication logic, while memory traffic volume has negligible impact on total package power.
Architectures and runtimes should evaluate on-chip reuse and reduced memory traffic, counting accesses at their actual width and arithmetic operations to determine the energy savings.

questions.q: The conservation-of-complexity heuristic is an exact physical conservation law of computer science that proves every simplification in an ML pipeline interface creates an identical, mathematically equal compensating burden in another component.
questions.explanation: False. The conservation-of-complexity heuristic (analogous to Tesler's Law in UI design) is a diagnostic design heuristic, not an exact physical conservation law. While simplifying one interface often displaces work elsewhere (e.g., shorter user prompts shifting parsing and retrieval burdens into system prompts and vector lookups, or INT8 quantization adding validation burden), good engineering design can eliminate accidental complexity outright without creating equal compensating costs. Its value is diagnostic: prompting engineers to trace where validation, state, or operational burdens move after simplifying a component.
questions.hint: Think about: distinguish the conservation-of-complexity diagnostic heuristic from exact physical conservation laws.

questions.q: The thirteen quantitative principles are unified by a central meta-heuristic known as the ____ heuristic, which reminds engineers that simplifying one interface often displaces validation, state, or operational burdens to another part of the system.
questions.explanation: conservation of complexity (or conservation-of-complexity). The conservation-of-complexity heuristic serves as a diagnostic lens connecting Foundations, Build, Optimize, and Deploy. It prompts engineers to trace where costs land after optimizing or abstracting an individual component.
questions.hint: Think about: identify the conservation-of-complexity heuristic as the overarching diagnostic framework uniting the thirteen quantitative principles.
answer: conservation of complexity (or conservation of complexity)
